questions.stem: An 18-year-old man presented with fatigue, malaise, and sore throat, nausea, and anorexia. He could not recall any sick contacts. On examination, there was an exudative pharyngitis and tender splenomegaly. Investigations: Group A streptococcus rapid antigen negative CMV IgM positive Heterophile antibody positive EBV testing: VCA IgM positive VCA IgG positive EA IgG positive EBNA IgG negative
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely etiologic agent?
questions.explanation: EBV The serologic results and heterophile antibody test support the diagnosis of EBV infection. IgM and IgG antibodies to the viral capsid antigen (VCA) are usually positive at the onset of symptoms, as are IgG antibodies to the early antigen (EA). EBNA antibodies, however, appear weeks later and then persist. They should be negative in the early stages of clinical illness, as they are here. Exudative pharyngitis in EBV can be confused for S. pyogenes, though rapid testing is negative. Of note a back-up culture or NAAT test should be performed to confirm the rapid test. CMV IgM is most likely a cross-reaction as IgM can cross-react with EBV VCA.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q3

questions.stem: A 19-year-old male presented to the student health clinic with several days of fever, sore throat, and profound fatigue. He has evident tonsillitis on exam and has some palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. The provider suspected possible streptococcal pharyngitis and prescribed amoxicillin. The next day he developed a pruritic, maculopapular rash.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his illness?
questions.explanation: Epstein–Barr virus This patient most likely has infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV . He has tonsillitis with prominent adenopathy and fatigue. Splenomegaly may also be identified on exam, and laboratory evaluation can show atypical lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia, and hepatitis. Patients with active EBV infection may develop drug eruptions when prescribed penicillins.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q29

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

questions.question: PCR question about increased sensitivity and differentiating active from latent infection due to viruses.

parts.text: What are 2 clinical indications for the use of EBV PCR to diagnose active infection.
What are 2 clinical indications for the use of CMV PCR to diagnose active infection.

questions.model_answer: a) EBV PCR indications (2): (1) Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) screening/diagnosis in solid organ or HSCT recipients. (2) CNS lymphoma diagnosis in HIV/AIDS patients (EBV DNA in CSF). b) CMV PCR indications (2): (1) Monitoring for CMV reactivation/disease in solid organ and HSCT transplant recipients (preemptive therapy guidance). (2) Diagnosis of CMV end-organ disease (e.g. colitis, retinitis) or congenital CMV infection.

questions.question: EBV

parts.text: Table: For each of the following state whether they are present or absent at the time of presentation for infectious Mononucleosis, and the duration of persistence - VCA IgM
Table: For each of the following state whether they are present or absent at the time of presentation for infectious Mononucleosis, and the duration of persistence - VCA IgG
Table: For each of the following state whether they are present or absent at the time of presentation for infectious Mononucleosis, and the duration of persistence - EBV Nuclear Antigen
List 4 cancers caused by EBV

questions.model_answer:
VCA IgM: present at presentation of acute infectious mononucleosis; short-lived, typically becomes undetectable within 4-6 weeks (marker of acute/recent infection).
VCA IgG: present at presentation (appears early, near symptom onset) and persists for life (marker of past infection/immunity once IgM has cleared).
EBV Nuclear Antigen (EBNA): absent at presentation - it does not appear until convalescence, roughly 6-12 weeks after infection - but then persists for life; its absence with positive VCA IgG helps confirm recent/acute infection.
Four EBV-associated cancers: Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, PTLD.

questions.question: A patient is awaiting a kidney transplant. He is EBV negative. A donor kidney is available, and the donor's serology is VCA IgM neg, VCA IgG pos, EBNA pos.

parts.text: Interpret the serology
What are the clinical implications of transplanting into an EBV negative host?

questions.model_answer:
a) Serology interpretation: VCA IgM negative, VCA IgG positive, EBNA positive - donor has had past (remote) EBV infection and is immune; there is no evidence of acute/recent infection.
b) Clinical implication of transplanting an EBV-seropositive organ into an EBV-seronegative (naive) recipient: this is a donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R-) mismatch, the highest-risk scenario for primary EBV infection after transplant, since latently infected donor lymphocytes can transmit EBV to the naive recipient under immunosuppression. This significantly increases the risk of posttransplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD); such patients warrant close EBV viral-load monitoring post-transplant, with consideration of reduced immunosuppression if PTLD develops.

parts.text: Name 6 different viruses that cause cancer and what type of cancer?

questions.model_answer: (1) Human papillomavirus (HPV) - cervical, anal, vulvar/vaginal/penile, and oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. (2) Hepatitis B virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (3) Hepatitis C virus - hepatocellular carcinoma. (4) Epstein-Barr virus - Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin lymphoma. (5) Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8/KSHV) - Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, multicentric Castleman disease. (6) Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) - adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (Merkel cell polyomavirus causing Merkel cell carcinoma is another acceptable answer).

questions.question: Viral table

parts.text: Complete the table (Nucleic Acid, Envelope, Antiviral) for: Mumps, Measles, Hepatitis B, EBV, Ebola, Zika

questions.model_answer: Mumps: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care only). Measles: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; no specific antiviral (supportive care; ribavirin has been used off-label in severe cases). Hepatitis B: partially double-stranded DNA, enveloped; antivirals - tenofovir, entecavir (also lamivudine/adefovir/telbivudine). EBV: double-stranded DNA, enveloped; no specific approved antiviral for routine infection (ganciclovir/valganciclovir used off-label for select EBV-driven disease). Ebola virus: single-stranded negative-sense RNA, enveloped; antivirals - monoclonal antibody cocktails (e.g., REGN-EB3/inmazeb, ansuvimab) and remdesivir has been studied. Zika virus: single-stranded positive-sense RNA, enveloped; no approved antiviral (supportive care only).

questions.question: Regarding post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder:

parts.text: What are 2 risk factors for this condition?
What test can be performed on a lymph node biopsy that will support this diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: a) Two risk factors for PTLD: (1) EBV donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R-) serostatus mismatch (highest risk group). (2) Transplantation of lymphoid-rich organs (e.g. intestine, lung) compared with kidney/heart/liver, due to greater load of infected donor B cells transferred with the graft; degree of immunosuppression is also a major risk factor. b) Test on lymph node biopsy supporting diagnosis: EBER (EBV-encoded RNA) in situ hybridization on the biopsy tissue, demonstrating EBV within the lymphoproliferative tissue, along with histopathology showing polymorphic or monomorphic lymphoproliferation.
